title: Reading comprehension: birds and runways
text:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

Every year, airfields record a large number of collisions between aircraft and birds. Most of them happen close to the ground, during take-off and landing, when an aircraft is low and slow and the birds are busy feeding. A kite weighing a little over a kilogram can crack a windscreen or damage an engine if it is struck at high speed.

Airfield staff therefore treat bird control as a daily duty rather than an occasional chore. Grass beside the runway is kept short, since tall grass hides insects and small animals that attract birds. Open garbage dumps near the boundary are reported to the local authorities, because they draw flocks from miles around. Some airfields play recorded distress calls of birds, while others use trained teams who walk the runway before the first flight of the day. No single method works for long, because birds soon learn to ignore a sound or a scarecrow that never changes. The safest airfields keep changing their methods and keep careful records of every sighting.

title: Reading comprehension: the village that went solar
text:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

For years the evenings in Sundarpur ended early. Power cuts were common, and families depended on kerosene lamps that filled the rooms with smoke and made reading difficult. When the village council proposed fixing solar panels on the roof of the school and the health centre, many elders were doubtful. They felt that a machine which needed no fuel could not be trusted.

The first monsoon proved them partly right. Cloudy days meant less power, and the batteries ran low by midnight. Instead of giving up, the council trained two young women to look after the system, clean the panels and keep a record of the power produced each day. They learned to switch off the less important loads on cloudy evenings so that the health centre always had light. Within two years, the school was running evening classes, and the elders who had laughed at the idea were among the first to ask for panels on their own homes.

title: Reading comprehension: working through the night
text:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

Many people believe that sleep is simply time lost, and that a determined person can do without it. Research on night-shift workers tells a different story. After about seventeen hours without sleep, a person's reaction time slows to a level similar to that of someone who has had an alcoholic drink. The danger is that tired people rarely notice it themselves; they feel alert enough while making more and more small mistakes.

For this reason, organisations that work round the clock plan rest as carefully as they plan work. Duty hours are limited, crews are given a fixed period of rest between shifts, and a short nap before a long night is encouraged rather than mocked. The aim is not comfort but safety: a well-rested crew notices the warning light that a tired crew would miss.
